markdown:
Security hiring fails in a predictable way. A team opens a seat for a "security engineer," receives hundreds of applications that list the same tools, and cannot tell which candidates have actually handled an incident, tuned a detection or argued a risk decision with an engineering lead. This guide is for the people who have to make those calls: it covers how to scope the main roles, how to screen for practical skill, which skills are shifting and what keeps analysts from leaving.

It contains no market averages. Where a figure appears, it is an illustrative example with stated assumptions. For real data on supply and pay, go to the primary sources, such as the NICE Workforce Framework published by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology for role definitions and the Bureau of Labor Statistics for occupational wages.

## What are the main security roles, and how do they differ?

Start from the work the seat has to do in its first six months, then map it to a role family.

| Role family | Typical first-year work | A screening question that separates strong candidates |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Security operations analyst | Triage alerts, escalate, document incidents | "Walk me through the last alert you closed as benign and how you were sure." |
| Detection engineer | Write and tune detections, measure false positives | "How did you decide a rule was too noisy to keep?" |
| Incident responder | Lead containment, preserve evidence, write the post-incident review | "What did you change after your last incident?" |
| Cloud security engineer | Review configurations, set guardrails, manage identity policy | "How would you find a public storage bucket nobody owns?" |
| Application security engineer | Threat-model features, review code, run the fix process with developers | "Describe a finding you persuaded a team to fix against their schedule." |
| Governance, risk and compliance analyst | Map controls to frameworks, prepare for audits, track exceptions | "How do you keep a control from becoming a ritual?" |

Write the role around outcomes and tools you actually use. A brief that lists every certification and every platform invites candidates who have touched everything and mastered nothing. Choose the two or three things the person must do on day one and mark the rest as learnable.

## How should you screen for practical skill?

Credentials show that someone studied. They do not show how a person behaves at three in the morning with partial logs. Add one short exercise to the process and keep it the same for every candidate in a role.

- **For analysts:** give a small log excerpt and ask the candidate to describe what they would check next and what they would escalate. Score their reasoning, not whether they land on a single answer.
- **For detection engineers:** hand over a noisy rule and ask how they would reduce false positives without missing the behaviour you care about.
- **For cloud and application roles:** a short design review of a sample architecture, where the candidate identifies the most important risk and what they would fix first.
- **For GRC roles:** a policy that does not match practice. Ask what they would do about the gap.

Keep exercises under an hour, tell candidates what is being assessed and pay for anything longer. A strong candidate with options will drop out of a long unpaid take-home.

## Which skills are shifting?

**AI-assisted triage.** Tools that summarise alerts, correlate events and draft case notes are becoming common. The human work that remains is judging whether the summary is right, noticing what the tool could not see and deciding when to escalate. Ask candidates how they check an automated conclusion before acting on it.

**Cloud and identity.** A growing share of incidents turn on credentials, permissions and misconfiguration rather than on a single endpoint. Hire for comfort reading identity policies and cloud audit logs.

**Detection as engineering.** Writing a detection, testing it, measuring noise and retiring it when it stops helping is a software discipline. Candidates who version-control their detections and write tests for them usually bring that habit to the whole team.

**Communicating risk.** Security staff spend a large part of their time persuading others. Look for someone who can state a risk in one sentence, say what it would cost to fix and recommend a decision.

**AI systems as an asset to defend.** If your company ships or uses models, ask about prompt injection, data leakage and access controls around model tooling. Do not require expertise that few people have; look for people who reason clearly about new attack surfaces.

## What do you owe candidates on compensation?

Security pay varies widely with specialism, clearance, location and company stage, and published roundups often disagree. Build your range from your own bands, public wage data and the reasons candidates decline. If you hold a security clearance requirement, say so in the first message; it narrows the pool and candidates need to know before they invest time.

Be careful with premium claims for scarce skills. If a niche skill is genuinely scarce, you will see it in your own pipeline: few qualified applicants and repeated declines on pay.

## Why do security professionals leave?

The patterns below recur, but check them against your own exit conversations.

- **Alert fatigue.** Analysts who triage hundreds of low-value alerts a week are doing a job that detection engineering should have fixed. Measure the proportion of alerts that lead to action and treat a low figure as a work item.
- **On-call load.** An uneven rota concentrates burnout. Share it fairly, compensate it and protect rest after a night incident.
- **Blame after incidents.** If post-incident reviews look for a culprit, people hide mistakes. Blameless reviews with concrete actions keep information flowing.
- **No route beyond analyst work.** Give analysts a visible path into detection engineering, incident response or cloud security, with time to learn.
- **Security as the "department of no."** People who are routinely overruled and never told why become disengaged. Record risk decisions and who accepted them.

## What does on-call really cost? An illustrative example

Suppose a team of six analysts runs a 24-hour rota with one person on call per week, and each on-call week involves two night-time pages. Assume, purely for the example, that each night-time page costs three hours of broken sleep and that the team gives a half day of recovery after each one. Over a year that is roughly 104 pages and 104 half days, or 52 working days of recovery time, spread across six people. The point of the arithmetic is not the totals; it is that the cost is visible and can be set against the cost of replacing someone who leaves because the rota is unfair. Use your own numbers.

## A 90-day plan for a new security hire

Give the new hire access in week one, a single contained task by the end of the first month, and a written first-90-day goal agreed with their manager. Shadow an incident or a tabletop exercise in the first quarter. Ask them at 30 and 90 days what slowed them down; you will learn more about your onboarding than from any survey.
